commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.

commands.name: doctor

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read FIRST, before you answer, run a command or open a file (already started? read it now); don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file; if nothing hits, load this skill).

content.text:
**The Tidewater Light**

The beach below Harrow Point was not a beach people visited. It was a shelf of black rock and gravel, scoured by the north current, and for thirty-one years Ada Quill had walked it every morning at low tide with a canvas bag over one shoulder and her eyes on the wrack line.

The lighthouse had been automated the year before she came. The lamp turned by itself now, and the foghorn sounded when a sensor said so. But the Coast Guard still paid a keeper to check the lens, scrub the gallery windows, log the weather, and keep the stairs swept, and Ada had taken the post because it left her mornings free and her evenings quiet. Nobody had asked her to be useful beyond that. She had decided, somewhere in her first winter, that the sea glass was her own business.

It came in the way it always had. Bottles broken on rocks, and then the sea doing the slow work of grinding edges into softness. Cobalt from medicine bottles. Brown from beer, which was common and which she kept anyway. Aqua from old soda, pale green from window panes, and the rare, thrilling red that was almost always from a lantern lens or a road reflector. Ada had a rule that she would only pick up pieces smaller than her palm and larger than a fingernail, and that she would never dig for them. The sea offered, and she accepted. That was the whole philosophy, and she thought it was a good one for a keeper.

The morning in question was gray and still. A thin fog hung over the water, and the lamp above her had gone quiet for the day. She walked the high tide line with her head down, turning over kelp and bladderwrack, and found three pieces of cobalt, a sliver of white milk glass, and a small, perfectly round green stone that felt warm in her palm, though she knew that was only the sun she had not yet seen.

She was crouched, examining the green piece against the light, when she heard the boy.

He was perhaps eight, in a yellow raincoat too big for him, standing at the edge of the rocks where the path came down from the cliff road. His mother's voice floated down from above, calling him back. He did not go back. He was staring at Ada's bag.

"Are those treasure?" he asked.

"Some of them," Ada said. "Depends who you ask."

He came down the rocks carefully, one hand out for balance, and crouched beside her without asking. His name was Theo, he told her, and he was visiting his grandmother in the cottage with the blue shutters. He had been told not to go near the water. He had not been told not to look at it.

Ada opened her palm and showed him the green stone. He touched it with one finger, the way people touch things in museums.

"Where did it come from?"

"A bottle, probably. Or a jar. Something somebody threw away a long time ago, and then the sea kept it and kept working on it until it stopped being sharp."

"Why does the sea do that?"

She had been asked this question before, by children and by adults who should have known better, and she had never found an answer that satisfied anyone. So she told him the truth instead. "Because it has time. More time than we do. And it doesn't mind waiting."

Theo considered this with great seriousness. Then he said, "Can I have one?"

Ada thought about the rule. She thought about her thirty-one years of walking this shelf, and about how many pieces she had kept and how many she had let go. She thought about the lamp above them, turning in its cage of glass, guiding ships that would never know her name.

"You can find your own," she said. "That's the only way it counts."

He searched for twenty minutes with his whole body, flipping stones and squinting into the wet gravel, and came up with a piece of brown that he was delighted by and a shard of blue that he was even more delighted by. Ada didn't tell him the brown was common. He held the blue up to the fog, and the light came through it the color of a deep summer sea.

When his mother's voice came again, sharper this time, he stood and brushed off his knees. "I'll come back tomorrow," he said.

"The tide will be different tomorrow," Ada said. "You'll find different things."

He nodded as if this were the best news he'd heard all week, then scrambled up the rocks, shouting to his mother about the blue one.

Ada stayed crouched for a while after he was gone. The fog was lifting slowly off the water, and far out a single fishing boat was coming home. She opened her bag and dropped in the green stone, the three cobalt pieces, and the milk glass. Then she stood, shouldered the bag, and climbed back toward the lighthouse, where the lamp would turn again tonight whether anyone needed it or not.

At the top of the stairs she set the bag on the sill of the gallery window and unpacked her treasures onto a folded cloth, the way she always did. Lined up in the grey light, they looked like nothing much. A few dull fragments of things people had stopped wanting.

She picked up the green stone, held it to the window, and watched the sun finally break through the fog, filling it with light.

Tomorrow, she thought, she would walk the shelf again and see what the tide had brought in. It would be different. It always was.
